# Results — Study 380 (Curve-Roll-Down)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). "Riding the yield
curve" — buy a bond on a **steep** curve, hold a year, and (if the curve doesn't
move) collect its **carry** plus a **roll-down** price gain as the bond ages to a
lower-yield point. We test the claim that this reliably beats cash on the **real
Treasury curve** (constant-maturity yields), comparing the textbook *promised* roll+carry
to the **realized** excess-over-cash once the curve actually moves. Offline & deterministic;
run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily constant-maturity Treasury yields — `^IRX` (13-wk), `^FVX` (5y), `^TNX` (10y), `^TYX` (30y); public, no key |
| Window | 1990-01-02 → 2026-06-18 (**9,152** trading days; **36.5** years) |
| Sleeve | a **5-year** duration sleeve (mod. duration ≈ 4.5); cash = the 13-week bill (`^IRX`) |
| Realized return | 1y total ≈ `y0 − D·Δy` (carry minus duration P&L from the *actual* yield move); excess = total − cash |
| Entry / costs | 1-day execution lag; one-way 2 bps on ~1× annual roll turnover |
| Inference | **Newey-West HAC** *t* (252-lag) on overlapping annual windows; steep-curve placebo (20,000 draws) |

> **Period caveat (named on the Signal axis).** 1990–2026 is a **secular bond bull**:
> the 5y yield fell from ~8% to ~4%, a mean drift of **−0.13 pts/yr** that is a one-way
> tailwind for any duration sleeve. That tailwind cannot repeat starting from today's
> levels, so a full-sample edge that *depends* on it is regime-survivorship, not a law.

## The promise vs the reality — roll-down is a *static-curve* concept

The brochure number (from today's curve, before any rate move) vs what the sleeve actually
earned once the curve moved over the next year.

| quantity | value (per yr) |
|---|--:|
| **Promised** roll + carry (textbook, static curve) | **+4.76%** |
| **Realized** total return of the sleeve | **+4.33%** |
| Gap (= the curve moving) | **+0.43pp** |
| **Realized excess over cash** | **+1.65%** |

The realized **excess over cash** of the always-on 5y sleeve is **+1.65%/yr** (Sharpe
**0.34**, win-rate **63%**). Net of 2 bps on the annual roll it is **+1.63%** — costs are
negligible. So far this looks like a real, if modest, edge.

## The decisive cut — it is a non-repeatable secular tailwind

The full-sample HAC *t* crosses the bar; sub-periods show why that is **regime
survivorship**, not a robust signal.

| window | n | mean excess | Sharpe | mean Δy (5y) | **HAC t** |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1990–2009 | 5,264 | **+2.84%** | 0.58 | −0.33 | **3.46** |
| 2010–2026 | 3,886 | **+0.16%** | 0.04 | +0.12 | **0.17** |
| **Full (1990–2026)** | 8,899 | **+1.65%** | 0.34 | −0.13 | **2.46** |

Read it carefully. The full-sample HAC *t* of **2.46** would, taken alone, read REAL — but
it is **entirely** the 1990–2009 leg (*t* = 3.46), when yields fell **−0.33 pts/yr** and
duration was paid to be long. **Strip the secular bond bull and the edge is gone**:
2010–2026, with rates *rising* on net, the realized excess is **+0.16%/yr at t = 0.17**.
The roll-down "edge" is the **duration term premium** harvested in a one-way rate-decline
regime. (Note the *naive* t is **31.9** — overlapping annual windows badly overstate
significance; the **HAC** correction is what makes the honest test borderline-then-fragile.)

## The free lunch the curve takes back — regime split

Roll-down assumes a *static* curve. Splitting realized excess by whether the sleeve yield
actually **fell** (roll-down realized) or **rose** (roll-down erased):

| regime | n | mean realized excess |
|---|--:|--:|
| yield **fell** over the year (tailwind) | 4,968 | **+5.09%** |
| yield **rose** over the year (headwind) | 3,931 | **−2.70%** |

When rates rise — a hiking cycle, a bear-steepening — the duration P&L (`−D·Δy`) swamps the
carry+roll and the sleeve **loses** to cash. The promised roll-down is a static-curve
fiction; a single rising-rate year is enough to give it all back and then some.

## Does steepness add anything beyond being long duration? — placebo

Holding the sleeve only when the entry curve is in its **steepest tercile** vs random
timing of the same size:

| | mean excess |
|---|--:|
| steepest-tercile entries (k = 2,967) | **+3.28%** |
| random same-size draws (placebo mean) | +1.65% |
| placebo p (random ≥ steep) | **0.000** |

Steep entries *do* out-earn random ones (p ≈ 0) — but that is mechanical: a steeper curve
**is** more carry and more roll, i.e. more term premium to harvest. It is not evidence the
slope predicts anything beyond simply taking duration risk when it is best paid. The
positive-control below isolates exactly this.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful, carry alone is not an edge

A deterministic curve where the slope's predictive power **beyond** the mechanical carry
baseline is a known knob `edge`. The control regresses the carry-stripped excess on the
lagged slope rank and reports the HAC *t* of the slope coefficient:

| planted edge | recovered β | HAC t |
|---|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (carry baseline only) | −0.002 | **−0.63** |
| **+0.05** (genuine extra edge) | +0.049 | **19.2** |

With **no** planted edge the test does **not** fire (t = −0.63): a bare carry baseline —
exactly what a steep curve mechanically pays — is **not** a slope edge. A genuine planted
edge is recovered almost exactly (β ≈ 0.05) and lights up. The control proves the
measurement is unbiased **and** that "steep curves earn more" is the carry baseline, not a
predictive signal — precisely the trap the real tape falls into.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The realized excess-over-cash of a 5y sleeve is positive
  (**+1.65%/yr**) and the full-sample HAC *t* (**2.46**) just clears the bar — but it is
  **entirely** the 1990–2009 secular bond bull (*t* = 3.46); post-2010, with rates rising,
  it collapses to **+0.16%/yr at t = 0.17**. The "edge" is the duration term premium
  harvested in a non-repeatable one-way rate decline. Regime-survivorship, not a robust
  law ⇒ **WEAK**, not REAL.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Costs are negligible (2 bps), but the sleeve is **pure
  duration risk**: it earns **+5.1%/yr** when rates fall and **−2.7%/yr** when they rise,
  with a gross Sharpe of only **0.34**. The slope-timing overlay doesn't separate from
  simply being long duration. A levered carry trade a hiking cycle wipes out is **not** a
  NAV-scale free lunch.
- **Free lunch? — BUSTED.** Roll-down is sold as a static-curve certainty; the curve takes
  it back the moment rates move. Promised **+4.76%** roll+carry, realized total **+4.33%**,
  and a single rising-rate year flips the excess negative. The "ride the curve" pitch is
  the **term premium in a costume** — real when duration is paid, a loss when it isn't.
